problem: A company has grown from one office to five branches, each with its own subnet, plus a data center and an internet edge connecting to two ISPs. Every router needs to know how to reach every other subnet.
Manually typing a static route on every router for every subnet works for two routers — it does not survive a company with dozens of subnets and links that change over time.

Worse, static routes do not react to failure. If a link goes down, a statically configured router keeps trying to send traffic out the dead path until a human notices and edits the configuration. In an enterprise network, that means outages measured in the time it takes an engineer to log in, not the seconds a network should take to reroute automatically.

Dynamic routing protocols solve both problems: routers automatically learn about every reachable subnet from their neighbors, and automatically recalculate a new path within seconds of a failure — no manual intervention required.
concept: A routing protocol is a set of rules routers use to exchange information about network reachability with each other, so each router can build a routing table without a human typing every route by hand. This session gives the overview layer; OSPF, EIGRP, and BGP each get their own dedicated deep-dive in a later pass of the roadmap where relevant — this session's job is to build the map that connects them.
IGP — Interior Gateway Protocol: runs inside a single organization's network (a single Autonomous System). Examples: OSPF, EIGRP, IS-IS, RIP.

EGP — Exterior Gateway Protocol: runs between different organizations' networks (between Autonomous Systems), most notably the public internet. There is really only one EGP in production use today: BGP.

2.2 The three algorithm styles covered in this session Protocol Category Algorithm Scope OSPF Link-state IGP Dijkstra Shortest Path First (SPF) Within one organization (areas) EIGRP Advanced distance-vector / hybrid IGP (Cisco) DUAL (Diffusing Update Algorithm) Within one organization BGP Path-vector EGP Best-path selection over AS- Path attributes Between organizations (the internet)
deep: 3.1 OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) OSPF is an open-standard link-state protocol. Every router builds an identical topology database (the Link-State Database, built from Link-State Advertisements — LSAs) for its area, then independently runs Dijkstra's SPF algorithm against that database to compute the best path to every destination. Because every router calculates from the same complete map rather than trusting a neighbor's summarized opinion, OSPF converges fast and avoids many of the loop risks that plague simple distance-vector protocols.
Areas: OSPF networks are divided into areas to control LSA flooding scope; Area 0 (the backbone) is mandatory, and all other areas must connect to it, directly or via a virtual link.
Metric: cost, derived by default from interface bandwidth (100,000,000 / bandwidth in bps on Cisco IOS) — lower cost wins.
Neighbor discovery: Hello packets sent to multicast 224.0.0.5, every 10 seconds on broadcast/point- to-point links (dead interval 40s), or 30 seconds on NBMA links.

On multi-access segments (like a shared Ethernet VLAN), OSPF elects a Designated Router (DR) and Backup Designated Router (BDR) to reduce the number of adjacencies needed, based on OSPF priority and, as a tiebreaker, router ID.

3.2 EIGRP (Enhanced Interior Gateway Routing Protocol) EIGRP was originally Cisco-proprietary; core mechanisms were later published, though it remains overwhelmingly deployed on Cisco gear. It is often called "advanced distance-vector" or "hybrid" because, unlike classic distance-vector protocols, it does not blindly trust a neighbor's advertised distance — it uses the DUAL algorithm to guarantee loop-free paths and to pre-compute backup routes.
Metric: a composite value calculated from Bandwidth, Delay, Reliability, and Load (Bandwidth and Delay are used by default).

Successor: the current best loop-free path. Feasible Successor: a pre-computed, guaranteed loop-free backup path that can be installed instantly (near-zero convergence time) without waiting for a full recalculation.
Neighbor discovery: Hello packets via multicast 224.0.0.10, matching Autonomous System Number required to form a neighbor relationship.

3.3 BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) BGP is a path-vector protocol — instead of just a distance metric, each route carries the actual list of Autonomous Systems (AS-PATH) it has traversed, which both prevents loops (a router rejects any route that already lists its own AS in the path) and gives huge flexibility for policy-based routing decisions.
Runs over TCP port 179 (unlike OSPF and EIGRP, which run directly over IP) — this means BGP sessions are reliable, ordered, and can span non-directly-connected routers.
eBGP: between routers in different Autonomous Systems (external). iBGP: between routers in the same Autonomous System (internal), used to carry externally-learned routes across a large organization.

Key path-selection attributes, roughly in order of influence: Weight (Cisco-local) → Local Preference → AS-Path length → Origin → MED → eBGP over iBGP → lowest IGP metric to next hop → lowest router ID.

BGP is the only protocol that actually runs the public internet's default-free zone — every ISP and large enterprise with multiple internet connections uses BGP to exchange reachability for their public IP space.
workflow: 4.1 OSPF adjacency workflow 1. Down → Init: router hears a Hello from a neighbor.
2. Init → 2-Way: neighbor's Hello lists this router's ID back — bidirectional communication confirmed.
3. 2-Way → ExStart/Exchange: routers (on point-to-point or DR/BDR links) exchange Database Description packets summarizing their LSDB.
4. Exchange → Loading: routers request any LSAs they are missing via Link-State Request packets.
5. Loading → Full: LSDBs are identical; each router independently runs SPF and installs best routes into the routing table.
4.2 EIGRP DUAL workflow (on a link failure) 1. Router loses its Successor route (e.g., interface goes down).
2. If a Feasible Successor already exists in the topology table, it is installed immediately — sub-second convergence, no query needed.
3. If no Feasible Successor exists, the router goes "Active" for that route and sends queries to all neighbors asking for an alternate path.
4. Once all neighbors reply, DUAL selects the new loop-free Successor and the route returns to "Passive" (stable) state.
4.3 BGP path decision workflow (simplified) 1. Router receives multiple advertisements for the same prefix from different peers.
2. BGP runs its ordered best-path algorithm (Weight → Local Pref → AS-Path length → Origin → MED → eBGP>iBGP → IGP metric → Router ID) to pick exactly one best path.
3. The best path is installed in the routing table and advertised onward to other BGP peers, each of whom repeats their own best-path selection.
enterprise: OSPF — the default choice inside most medium-to-large enterprise campus and data center networks; vendor-neutral, well understood, works across mixed Cisco/non-Cisco environments.
EIGRP — still common inside all-Cisco enterprise shops that value its very fast convergence and simpler configuration versus OSPF's area design.

BGP — used at the internet edge (talking to ISPs), between data centers over WAN/dark fiber, and increasingly inside very large data centers ("BGP in the data center" / EVPN designs) as the IGP-of- choice for massive Clos fabrics.

A very common real design: OSPF or EIGRP runs inside the enterprise as the IGP, while BGP runs only at the network's edge, redistributing a small number of summarized routes between the two worlds — this separation of concerns is a recurring interview and design topic.
6. Dependencies — What Routing Protocols Need Beneath Them
IPv4/IPv6 addressing and subnetting (Sessions 30–32) — routing protocols advertise and select paths to IP prefixes; nothing works without consistent addressing first.
Routing (Session 29) and the Routing Table concept — routing protocols are simply an automated way of populating the same routing table a static route would populate manually.
Switching/VLANs/LACP (Sessions 28, 33, 35) — the underlying Layer 2 links and logical interfaces that routing protocol Hellos and updates travel across.
TCP (for BGP specifically, Session 43, upcoming) — BGP's reliability depends on TCP's connection-oriented delivery.
7. Dependents — What Relies on Routing Protocols

NAT (Session 37, upcoming) and ACLs (Session 38, upcoming) both operate on traffic after routing has already decided the path — routing protocols determine which interface that traffic reaches those features on.
High Availability and Disaster Recovery designs (Layer 5, upcoming) — automatic failover across sites fundamentally depends on a routing protocol noticing a path failure and rerouting within seconds.

Load Balancing (Session 48, upcoming) — equal-cost multi-path (ECMP) routing, used by both OSPF and EIGRP/BGP, is a direct routing-protocol feature that spreads traffic across multiple equal- cost links.
VPN/IPSec site-to-site designs (Sessions 45–46) commonly run a routing protocol (often BGP) over the encrypted tunnel to dynamically advertise reachable subnets between sites.
security: An unauthenticated router speaking a routing protocol on your network is a serious risk: it can inject false routes, black-hole traffic, or redirect it for interception (a routing-protocol-level man-in-the-middle). Each protocol has a defense:

OSPF — supports neighbor authentication (plaintext, MD5, or, on modern IOS, SHA via key- chains); passive-interface should be applied to any interface facing end users so OSPF never forms an adjacency with an untrusted device.
EIGRP — supports MD5 or SHA authentication between neighbors via key-chains; also typically uses passive-interface on user-facing ports.

BGP — supports MD5 (TCP MD5 signature) session authentication; at internet scale, route filtering (prefix-lists, AS-path filters) and RPKI (Resource Public Key Infrastructure) are used to prevent route hijacking, where an AS falsely originates someone else's IP space.

General best practice across all three: only enable the routing protocol on interfaces that actually face trusted routers, and filter/summarize what is advertised so an internal misconfiguration cannot leak into a partner network or the internet.

Lower AD always wins: Connected = 0, Static = 1, eBGP = 20, EIGRP (internal) = 90, OSPF = 110, RIP = 120, EIGRP (external) = 170, iBGP = 200.
example: A regional bank runs OSPF as its campus and data center IGP across roughly 40 routers, with Area 0 as the data center core and each branch office as its own OSPF area to contain LSA flooding and keep SPF recalculation fast. At the internet edge, two border routers each run eBGP sessions to two different ISPs for redundancy, then redistribute a single default route (0.0.0.0/0) into OSPF so the rest of the network knows how to reach the internet — while carefully NOT redistributing the bank's internal OSPF routes into BGP, keeping internal topology invisible to the outside world.
cloud: Public cloud VPCs/VNets generally hide dynamic IGP routing from the customer — routing between subnets inside a VPC is handled automatically by the cloud provider's underlying fabric, not something you configure OSPF or EIGRP for.

BGP, however, is very much customer-facing in hybrid cloud connectivity: AWS Direct Connect, Azure ExpressRoute, and Google Cloud Interconnect all use BGP to dynamically exchange routes between an on-premises network and the customer's virtual network in the cloud, and SD-WAN overlays commonly run BGP between sites as well. Large cloud providers' own internal data center fabrics are also frequently built on BGP (running as the IGP inside a Clos fabric) rather than OSPF, because BGP scales to enormous numbers of routers more predictably.
automation: Ansible modules (cisco.ios.ios_ospfv2, cisco.ios.ios_bgp_global, cisco.ios.ios_eigrp_interfaces) push consistent routing configuration across many devices and can enforce standardized authentication and passive-interface settings.

Python with Netmiko/NAPALM parses show ip route / show ip bgp summary output for automated health-checking, alerting on neighbor flaps, or validating that expected prefixes are present after a maintenance window.

Route-analytics/monitoring tools (e.g., BGP looking-glass tools, NetFlow combined with routing table state) are used at ISP/large-enterprise scale to detect route leaks or hijacks automatically rather than relying on manual inspection.
Infrastructure as Code for BGP is common in modern data center automation (e.g., declarative EVPN/BGP fabric configuration pushed via CI/CD pipelines to switches).
career: OSPF (single-area and, at a conceptual level, multi-area) and EIGRP fundamentals are core CCNA 200- 301 exam topics, and Administrative Distance / route selection logic is one of the most frequently tested and interviewed concepts in networking generally. BGP is typically outside CCNA depth but is a standard topic at CCNP/ISP-engineer level and is very often asked conceptually even in generalist infrastructure interviews ("what's the difference between an IGP and BGP" is a common screening question).

For the path toward an infrastructure/network engineer role, being able to whiteboard the OSPF adjacency states, explain why EIGRP converges faster via Feasible Successors, and explain why BGP is path-vector rather than distance-vector are all realistic technical-interview asks.
interview: Q1: What is the fundamental difference between a distance-vector and a link-state routing protocol?

A: A distance-vector protocol trusts a neighbor's advertised distance without seeing the full topology; a link-state protocol (like OSPF) builds a complete map of the topology on every router and independently computes the best path from it.
Q2: Two routes to the same prefix are learned via OSPF and EIGRP. Which one is installed, and why?
A: EIGRP, because its Administrative Distance (90 for internal EIGRP) is lower than OSPF's (110) — AD is compared before any metric, regardless of which protocol's path is technically "shorter."
Q3: Why does BGP use AS-Path instead of a simple hop count like RIP?

A: AS-Path both prevents routing loops (a router rejects a route that already contains its own AS) and enables policy-based route selection based on which organizations a path traverses, not just how many hops it takes.
Q4: Why is BGP described as an EGP while OSPF and EIGRP are IGPs?

A: BGP is designed to exchange routes between different administrative domains (Autonomous Systems), such as between two companies or ISPs; OSPF and EIGRP are designed to run within a single organization's network.
Q5: What allows EIGRP to converge faster than OSPF after a link failure in many cases?

A: EIGRP can pre-compute a loop-free backup path (a Feasible Successor) and install it immediately, without needing to query neighbors or recompute the whole topology, unlike a full SPF recalculation.
Q6: Why would an enterprise redistribute only a default route from BGP into OSPF instead of all internet routes?

A: Carrying the full internet routing table (800,000+ prefixes) inside an internal IGP would overwhelm router memory/CPU and is unnecessary — internal routers only need to know "send unknown destinations toward the edge," which a single default route accomplishes.
misconceptions: "The protocol with the lowest metric always wins." — False; Administrative Distance is compared first, between different protocols. Metric only breaks ties within the same protocol.

"OSPF is always better than EIGRP because it's a standard." — Not universally true; EIGRP often converges faster and is simpler to configure in same-vendor networks, which is why it's still deployed by choice, not just legacy inertia.

"BGP is just a bigger version of OSPF." — False; BGP is a fundamentally different algorithm family (path-vector, policy-driven, TCP-based) built for scale and trust boundaries between organizations, not for finding the mathematically shortest path within one network.

"Dynamic routing protocols eliminate the need for any static routes." — False; static default routes and floating static backups are still commonly used alongside dynamic protocols, especially at the network edge.

"More routing protocols running at once means better redundancy." — Not necessarily; running multiple IGPs without careful redistribution control is a common cause of routing loops and is generally avoided unless there's a clear migration or boundary reason.
anchors: OSPF = a cartographer. Every router draws the exact same complete map (LSDB) and independently calculates the shortest route on it — nobody has to trust anyone else's opinion, they trust the map.

EIGRP = a driver with a pre-planned detour already memorized. If the main road closes, they don't stop to ask for directions (query neighbors) — they already know a guaranteed-safe backup route (Feasible Successor) and take it instantly.

BGP = an immigration checkpoint. Every route carries a stamped passport (AS-Path) showing every country (Autonomous System) it passed through; a router rejects any route whose passport already has its own country stamped on it, which is exactly how it prevents loops.
Administrative Distance mnemonic: "Con-Stat-eB-EI-O-R-eE-iB" (0-1-20-90-110-120-170-200) — lower always wins, connected and static are always trusted over anything dynamic.

19. Lab — Hands-On Environment: GNS3 or Packet Tracer with three Cisco IOS routers (R1, R2, R3) connected in a triangle, building directly on prior CCNA Packet Tracer subnetting/VLSM work already completed.
Part A — OSPF single-area:
1. Address all three router-to-router links from a VLSM plan and enable OSPF process 1 on every interface with network ... area 0.
2. Verify adjacencies with show ip ospf neighbor — confirm all show state FULL.
3. Check show ip route on each router and confirm every subnet appears with an O code.
4. Shut down the direct link between R1 and R2 and confirm traffic reroutes via R3 within a few seconds.
Part B — EIGRP comparison (separate lab instance or VRF):
1. Reconfigure the same topology with router eigrp 100 and matching network statements on all three routers.
2. Verify neighbors with show ip eigrp neighbors and inspect the topology table with show ip eigrp topology to identify any Feasible Successors.
3. Fail the same link as in Part A and time the reconvergence — compare it against the OSPF result to build intuition for the convergence-speed discussion in Section 15.
Part C — conceptual only (BGP requires either a second AS or an internet-facing lab, so this is a config-writing exercise rather than a full lab):

Write out (on paper or in a text file) the router bgp <ASN>, neighbor <ip> remote-as <ASN>, and network statements needed to establish an eBGP session between R3 (acting as your edge router) and a simulated ISP router in a different AS — this builds the muscle memory for Layer 5's enterprise-services sessions without needing real internet transit.
